target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Cybersecurity) and Tech Enthusiasts

sections.title: The Tracing Dilemma
sections.content: Introduction to the conflict between public health (tracking virus spread) and individual privacy (data security). Explain why centralized databases are risky (potential for government surveillance).
sections.example: Imagine Alice and Bob are in a park. If Bob gets sick later, how can Alice be notified without a central server knowing exactly where they were or who they are?

sections.title: Prerequisite: The One-Way Hash & Bluetooth RSSI
sections.content: Briefly explain Cryptographic Hash Functions (generating a unique digital fingerprint that can't be reversed) and Bluetooth Low Energy (using signal strength/RSSI to estimate distance between devices).
sections.example: Visual: A meat grinder icon. Put in a secret word (Input), get out a random string (Hash). You can't turn the string back into the word.

sections.title: Phase 1: Generating Ephemeral IDs (The Nicknames)
sections.content: Each phone generates a rotating Secret Key daily. From this, it derives 'Ephemeral IDs' (EphIDs) that change every 15 minutes using a hash function. This prevents 'stalking' because the ID is constantly changing.
sections.example: Alice's phone creates a daily secret 'Sunlight'. Every 15 mins, it calculates Hash('Sunlight' + Time) to create IDs like 'A1x9', then 'B2z8'. She broadcasts these 'nicknames' via Bluetooth.

sections.title: Phase 2: The Digital Handshake
sections.content: When two phones are close, they exchange and store these EphIDs locally on the device (not a server). This is the 'Decentralized' part—the 'diary' of contacts stays on the phone.
sections.example: Alice and Bob sit on a bench. Alice's phone hears 'B2z8' and writes it in a private digital diary. Bob's phone hears 'A1x9' and does the same. Neither knows the other's real identity.

sections.title: Phase 3: Exposure Notification (The Bulletin Board)
sections.content: If Bob tests positive, he uploads his 'Secret Key' (not his location or contact list) to a public server. Everyone else's phone downloads the list of 'Infected Keys' and reconstructs the EphIDs to see if any match their local diary.
sections.example: Bob uploads his key 'Moonlight'. Alice's phone downloads it, calculates all possible IDs 'Moonlight' would have produced, and sees 'B2z8' matches an entry in her diary. Her phone alerts her: 'Potential Exposure!'

sections.title: Summary & Privacy Benefits
sections.content: Recap the flow: Local Generation -> Local Storage -> Voluntary Disclosure -> Local Matching. Emphasize that the server never knows 'who met whom' or 'where'.
sections.example: Comparison Chart: Centralized (Server knows all) vs. DP-3T (Server is just a bulletin board, intelligence stays at the edge/phones).
